pages.title: Answer Key - Week 18 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 18 Problem Set: Tangent Lines, Normals, and Vertical Tangents

Calculus Honors · Module 9. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. f(2) = 8−4+1 = 5. f'(x) = 3x²−2, so f'(2) = 10. Tangent: y−5 = 10(x−2), so y = 10x − 15. Normal slope = −1/10: y−5 = −(1/10)(x−2), so y = −x/10 + 26/5.
  2. g'(x) = 3x²−6x−9 = 3(x−3)(x+1) = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or x = −1. g(3) = 27−27−27+5 = −22; g(−1) = −1−3+9+5 = 10. Points: (3, −22) and (−1, 10).
  3. Check: 1+8 = 9 ✓. 3x² + 3y²y' = 0 ⇒ y' = −x²/y². At (1,2): −1/4. Tangent: y−2 = −(1/4)(x−1), i.e. y = −x/4 + 9/4. Normal slope 4: y−2 = 4(x−1), i.e. y = 4x − 2.
  4. Tangent at (a,a²): y = a² + 2a(x−a). Through (1,−3): −3 = a² + 2a(1−a) = 2a − a², so a²−2a−3 = 0 = (a−3)(a+1). a = 3: y = 9+6(x−3) = 6x−9. a = −1: y = 1−2(x+1) = −2x−1. Check: 6(1)−9 = −3 ✓ and −2(1)−1 = −3 ✓.
  5. f(0)=0, so the difference quotient is h^(1/3)/h = h^(−2/3) = 1/∛(h²). As h→0⁺ and as h→0⁻ this → +∞ (∛(h²) is positive and tends to 0). Both one-sided limits are +∞, so the slope is infinite in the same direction from both sides: a vertical tangent line, x = 0.
  6. h'(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) = 2/(3∛x). As x→0⁻, h' → −∞; as x→0⁺, h' → +∞. The slopes are infinite with opposite signs: both branches drop steeply into the origin, one from each side, forming a sharp point pointing down, a cusp. There is no single tangent line, whereas ∛x (problem 5) has slope +∞ on both sides and one vertical tangent.
  7. 2x + 2y·y' = 0 ⇒ y' = −x/y. Horizontal tangent: y' = 0 ⇒ x = 0 (y≠0): (0,5) and (0,−5). Vertical tangent: y = 0 so the denominator vanishes (and x = ±5 ≠ 0 so the numerator does not): (5,0) and (−5,0). At those points the formula is undefined because the slope is infinite, not because the curve is missing.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 19 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 19 Problem Set: Linear Approximation and Differentials

Calculus Honors · Module 9. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. f(4)=2, f'(x) = 1/(2√x), f'(4) = 1/4. L(x) = 2 + (x−4)/4. L(4.1) = 2.025, so √4.1 ≈ 2.025. L(3.9) = 1.975, so √3.9 ≈ 1.975.
  2. f(27)=3, f'(x) = 1/(3x^(2/3)), f'(27) = 1/27. L(x) = 3 + (x−27)/27 = x/27 + 2. L(26) = 3 − 1/27 ≈ 2.9630. Good base point: 27 is a perfect cube near 26, so f(a) and f'(a) are exact and easy, and x is only 1 away.
  3. ln: f(1)=0, f'(1)=1, L(x) = x − 1; ln(1.1) ≈ 0.1. eˣ: f(0)=1, f'(0)=1, L(x) = 1+x; e^0.05 ≈ 1.05.
  4. True values: √4.1 ≈ 2.02485 (estimate 2.025 is slightly above); √3.9 ≈ 1.97484 (estimate 1.975 slightly above); ∛26 ≈ 2.96250 (estimate 2.96296, above); ln 1.1 ≈ 0.09531 (estimate 0.1, above); e^0.05 ≈ 1.05127 (estimate 1.05, below). Picture: √ₓ, ∛ₓ and ln x bend downward, so their tangent lines lie above the curve; eˣ bends upward, so its tangent line lies below. (Full credit for linking above/below to which way the curve bends, a preview of concavity.)
  5. f'(x) = 3x²−2, f'(2) = 10, so dy = 10(0.05) = 0.5. Δy = f(2.05)−f(2) = (8.615125 − 4.1) − 4 = 0.515125. They differ by about 0.0151 (3%): dy is the change along the tangent line, Δy the change along the curve.
  6. V = (4/3)πr³, dV = 4πr² dr = 4π(25)(0.1) = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm³. V(5) = 500π/3 ≈ 523.6, so dV/V = 10π / (500π/3) = 0.06 = 6% (three times the 2% error in r, since V ∝ r³).
  7. L(100) = 2 + 96/4 = 26. True value: 10. The estimate is badly wrong because 100 is far from the base point 4 and √x bends away from its tangent line. A linear approximation is trustworthy only near the base point; the farther away, the more the curvature accumulates.

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 9 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 9 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 9. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. E(x)/(x−a) = [f(x)−f(a)]/(x−a) − f'(a). Since f is differentiable at a, the difference quotient → f'(a), so E(x)/(x−a) → f'(a)−f'(a) = 0. For M: E_M(x) = f(x) − f(a) − m(x−a), so E_M(x)/(x−a) = [f(x)−f(a)]/(x−a) − m → f'(a)−m ≠ 0. So the tangent line is the only line through the point whose error vanishes faster than the distance x−a: the error shrinks to zero even after dividing by the distance. Look for: the limit identified with the definition of the derivative, and the contrast with a wrong-slope line (whose error is only as small as the distance itself).

Part B. 3x² + 3y²y' = 6y + 6xy' ⇒ y'(3y²−6x) = 6y−3x² ⇒ y' = (2y−x²)/(y²−2x). At (3,3): (6−9)/(9−6) = −1. Check the point: 27+27 = 54 = 6·3·3 ✓. Tangent: y−3 = −(x−3), i.e. y = −x + 6. Normal slope 1: y = x. Horizontal tangent: numerator 2y−x² = 0 ⇒ y = x²/2. Substitute: x³ + x⁶/8 = 3x³ ⇒ x⁶/8 = 2x³ ⇒ x³ = 16 (x≠0) ⇒ x = 16^(1/3) = 2^(4/3) = 2∛2 ≈ 2.520, y = x²/2 = 2^(5/3) = 2∛4 ≈ 3.175. Exact point: (2∛2, 2∛4). Check the denominator: y²−2x = 2^(10/3) − 2^(7/3) = 2^(7/3)(2−1) ≠ 0 ✓. We must check it because a zero numerator gives a horizontal tangent only if the denominator is nonzero; if both were zero the slope would be undetermined, and if only the denominator were zero the tangent would be vertical.

Part C. V = x³: dV = 3x²dx = 3(100)(0.2) = 60 cm³; relative: 60/1000 = 6%. A = 6x²: dA = 12x dx = 12(10)(0.2) = 24 cm²; relative: 24/600 = 4%. Exact largest errors: ΔV = 10.2³−1000 = 1061.208−1000 = 61.208 cm³; ΔA = 6(10.2²−100) = 6(4.04) = 24.24 cm². The differentials slightly underestimate the exact errors (the curve bends upward away from the tangent line). Percent error is 3× the edge's 2% error for volume (V ∝ x³) but only 2× for area (A ∝ x²): dV/V = 3 dx/x, dA/A = 2 dx/x.

Part D. f(1)=1, f'(1)=2, L(x) = 1+2(x−1) = 2x−1. E(x) = x²−(2x−1) = x²−2x+1 = (x−1)². Doubling the distance from the base point quadruples the error (e.g., x=1.1 gives 0.01; x=1.2 gives 0.04). For |x| at 0: the difference quotient |h|/h is −1 from the left and +1 from the right, so f'(0) does not exist (a corner) and no line fits the graph near 0 with error vanishing faster than |x|; linearization requires differentiability. Contrast: ∛x has f'(0) = +∞ (vertical tangent, no finite slope for L), x^(2/3) has a cusp. What a linear approximation promises: near the base point the error is small relative to the distance; it does not promise a fixed error size far away (√100 ≈ 26 from base 4). Full credit for naming the local nature of the promise.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct implicit derivative, tangent/normal lines, differentials, exact error comparison.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): Part A uses the definition of the derivative; Part B checks the denominator; Part D distinguishes the three failure modes.
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, exact values (cube roots), labeled answers, units in Part C.
  • Intellectual honesty (4): states what a linear approximation guarantees and what it does not; candid about where an estimate cannot be trusted.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 20 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 20 Problem Set: Critical Points and the First Derivative Test

Calculus Honors · Module 10. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. f' = 3x²−12x+9 = 3(x−1)(x−3); critical points x = 1 and x = 3 (f' exists everywhere). f'(1) = f'(3) = 0; f(1) = 5, f(3) = 1.
  2. f' = (5/3)x^(2/3) − (10/3)x^(−1/3) = (5/3)x^(−1/3)(x−2) = 5(x−2) / (3x^(1/3)). f'(x)=0 at x = 2; f' is undefined at x = 0. x = 0 is critical because the definition requires only that c be in the domain of f (it is: f(0)=0) and that f'(c)=0 or not exist. (The graph has a cusp there.)
  3. f' = 3x²−6x+3 = 3(x−1)² = 0 only at x=1. Since (x−1)² ≥ 0, f'(x) ≥ 0 on both sides of 1 (f' > 0 for x<1 and for x>1). f' does not change sign, so f is increasing straight through x = 1 and there is no local extremum. (f(x) = (x−1)³+1, a shifted cubic.)
  4. f' = 4x³−16x = 4x(x−2)(x+2); critical points x = −2, 0, 2. Sign chart: f'<0 on (−∞,−2), f'>0 on (−2,0), f'<0 on (0,2), f'>0 on (2,∞) (test values −3, −1, 1, 3 give −60, 12, −12, 60). So local minimum at x=−2 (y = −13), local maximum at x=0 (y = 3), local minimum at x=2 (y = −13).
  5. Product Rule: f' = e⁻ˣ − xe⁻ˣ = (1−x)e⁻ˣ. Since e⁻ˣ > 0 always, the sign of f' is the sign of 1−x: increasing on (−∞,1), decreasing on (1,∞). f' changes + to − at x=1: local (indeed absolute) maximum f(1) = 1/e ≈ 0.368.
  6. f' = 1 − 4/x² = (x²−4)/x². Zero at x = ±2; x=0 is not in the domain, so it is not a critical point (it is a vertical asymptote). Sign: f'>0 on (−∞,−2), <0 on (−2,0), <0 on (0,2), >0 on (2,∞). Local max at x=−2, f(−2) = −4; local min at x=2, f(2) = 4. The local max (−4) is below the local min (4) because the graph has two separate branches separated by the asymptote; local extrema compare only with nearby points, not with the whole function.
  7. (a) At an interior local extremum with a derivative, the tangent line must be horizontal (otherwise f would still be rising or falling nearby), so f'(c)=0. Therefore extrema can only occur at critical points (or endpoints): look there first. (b) f(x)=x³ at c=0: f'(0)=0, but f is increasing through 0, so there is no extremum; the First Derivative Test reports no sign change in f' (f' = 3x² ≥ 0 on both sides). (Also acceptable: f(x)=(x−1)³+1 from problem 3.) Look for: "candidate, not guarantee."

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 21 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 21 Problem Set: Absolute Extrema and Reading Graphs

Calculus Honors · Module 10. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. f' = 3x²−6x = 3x(x−2); critical points x=0, 2 (both in (−1,4)). Table: f(−1) = −3; f(0) = 1; f(2) = −3; f(4) = 17. Absolute maximum 17 at x = 4; absolute minimum −3, attained at both x = −1 and x = 2.
  2. f' = (2/3)x^(−1/3) is never 0 but is undefined at x=0, which is in the domain and in the interval, so x=0 is a critical point. f(−1) = 1; f(0) = 0; f(8) = 4. Absolute maximum 4 at x=8; absolute minimum 0 at x=0. The cusp at 0 is invisible to the equation f'=0.
  3. f' = [(x²+1) − x·2x]/(x²+1)² = (1−x²)/(x²+1)²; zero at x=1 (x=−1 is outside [0,3]). f(0) = 0; f(1) = 1/2; f(3) = 3/10. Absolute maximum 1/2 at x=1; absolute minimum 0 at x=0.
  4. f' = 1 − 1/x²; on (0,∞) the only critical point is x=1. f'<0 on (0,1), f'>0 on (1,∞), so f(1) = 2 is a local minimum, and since f decreases all the way down to x=1 and increases after it, it is the absolute minimum, 2. As x→0⁺ and as x→∞, f(x)→∞, so f has no absolute maximum.
  5. The interval (0,1] is not closed (it omits 0), so the Extreme Value Theorem's hypothesis "continuous on a closed interval [a,b]" fails. Confirmation: f(x)=1/x increases without bound as x→0⁺, so no value is largest: no absolute maximum. It does have an absolute minimum, f(1) = 1 at x=1 (f is decreasing on (0,1]). Honest point: the theorem failing to apply does not mean there is never an extremum; it means there is no guarantee.
  6. Critical points in [0,6]: x=1 (f'=0): f' changes − to +, local minimum, f=0. x=3 (f' DNE): f' changes + to −, local maximum, f=4. x=5 (f'=0): f' changes − to +, local minimum, f=1. Closed Interval Method: compare f(0)=2, f(1)=0, f(3)=4, f(5)=1, f(6)=3. Absolute maximum 4 at x=3; absolute minimum 0 at x=1. The endpoints are not extrema here.
  7. Sample sketch: starts at (−2,1), rises to a smooth peak (0,3), falls to a sharp corner at (2,−1), then rises to (5,2). Absolute maximum 3 at x=0 (with no other critical points, f is monotonic between them: it rises from f(−2)=1 up to 3, falls to −1, then rises only to f(5)=2, so every value is at most 3). Absolute minimum −1 at x=2. Look for: a corner (not a smooth bottom) at x=2, f increasing on (2,5), and the endpoint values compared.

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 10 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 10 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 10. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. Choose a small interval (c−δ, c+δ) on which the sign conditions hold. Let x be in (c−δ, c). f is continuous on [x,c] (given) and differentiable on (x,c) with f'<0 there, so by the MVT (or Lesson 8.04's sign result) f(c)−f(x) = f'(t)(c−x) for some t in (x,c); the product is negative (f'(t)<0, c−x>0), so f(c) < f(x). Now let x be in (c, c+δ). f is continuous on [c,x] and differentiable on (c,x) with f'>0, so f(x)−f(c) = f'(t)(x−c) > 0, i.e., f(x) > f(c). So f(c) ≤ f(x) for every x near c: a local minimum. Look for: continuity at c used (not differentiability at c), hypotheses named for each side, and the sign of the product argued.

Part B. f' = (4/3)x^(1/3) − (4/3)x^(−2/3) = (4/3)x^(−2/3)(x−1) = 4(x−1) / (3x^(2/3)). Critical points: x = 1 (f'=0) and x = 0 (f' undefined, in the domain). Since x^(2/3) > 0 for x≠0, the sign of f' is the sign of x−1: f'<0 on (−∞,0), f'<0 on (0,1), f'>0 on (1,∞). At x=0, f' does not change sign: no extremum; f decreases through a point where the tangent line is vertical (f' → −∞ from both sides). At x=1, − to +: local minimum, f(1) = −3. Closed Interval Method on [−1,8]: f(−1) = 1 − 4(−1) = 5; f(0) = 0; f(1) = −3; f(8) = 16 − 8 = 8. Absolute maximum 8 at x=8; absolute minimum −3 at x=1.

Part C. f' = (x−1)(x−3)² = 0 at x=1 and x=3. Since (x−3)² ≥ 0, the sign of f' is the sign of x−1 (except it is 0 at x=3): f'<0 on (−∞,1), f'>0 on (1,3), f'>0 on (3,∞). So x=1 is a local (absolute) minimum; x=3 is not an extremum (f' does not change sign). f is increasing on [1,∞): for x₁<x₂ both in [1,3], the MVT on [x₁,x₂] gives t in (x₁,x₂), which lies inside (1,3) where f'>0, so f(x₁)<f(x₂); the same argument works on [3,∞); and if x₁<3<x₂ then f(x₁)<f(3)<f(x₂). A zero derivative at one point does not stop f from increasing. f' = x³−7x²+15x−9, so f(x) = x⁴/4 − 7x³/3 + 15x²/2 − 9x (f(0)=0 gives C=0). On [0,4]: f(0) = 0; f(1) = −43/12; f(3) = −9/4; f(4) = −4/3. Absolute maximum 0 at x=0; absolute minimum −43/12 at x=1.

Part D. (i) f(x)=x³ at 0 (f'(0)=0, f' = 3x² does not change sign). (ii) f(x)=|x| at 0 (f' does not exist: corner; f' changes − to +: local min). (iii) f(x)=x^(1/3) at 0 (f' = (1/3)x^(−2/3) undefined, vertical tangent, f' > 0 on both sides, no extremum). Accept any valid triples (e.g. x^(2/3) for (ii): cusp, local min). The reflection should say which is hardest and why (often (iii): the derivative is undefined, so students want to call it an extremum). Full credit for explaining that a critical point is a candidate that the First Derivative Test must confirm or reject.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct derivatives, critical points, classification, absolute extrema values.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): hypotheses (continuity at c, differentiability on each side) named; the vertical-tangent case at x=0 handled; sign argument for f increasing through f'(3)=0.
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, exact values, a clear value table, labeled answers.
  • Intellectual honesty (4): states what is proven and what is only checked; candid about which example is hardest to defend.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 22 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 22 Problem Set: Concavity and Inflection Points

Calculus Honors · Module 11. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. f' = 3x²−12x+9; f'' = 6x−12 = 6(x−2). f''<0 on (−∞,2): concave down; f''>0 on (2,∞): concave up. Concavity changes at x=2, f(2) = 8−24+18+1 = 3: inflection point (2, 3).
  2. f' = 4x³−12x; f'' = 12x²−12 = 12(x−1)(x+1). Sign chart: f''>0 on (−∞,−1), f''<0 on (−1,1), f''>0 on (1,∞). Concave up on (−∞,−1) and (1,∞); concave down on (−1,1). Inflection points at x=±1, with f(±1) = 1−6 = −5: (−1,−5) and (1,−5).
  3. f'' = 12x² ≥ 0 for all x, so f'' does not change sign at 0: f is concave up on both sides, no inflection point at 0. g'' = 6x is negative for x<0 and positive for x>0: concavity changes, so g has an inflection point at (0,0). f''(0)=0 only says the second derivative might change sign there; the sign change is what defines an inflection point.
  4. f' = e⁻ˣ − xe⁻ˣ = (1−x)e⁻ˣ; f'' = −e⁻ˣ − (1−x)e⁻ˣ = (x−2)e⁻ˣ. Since e⁻ˣ>0, the sign of f'' is the sign of x−2: concave down on (−∞,2), concave up on (2,∞). Inflection point (2, 2e⁻²) ≈ (2, 0.271).
  5. f' = 3x²−6x−9 = 3(x−3)(x+1), so critical points at x=3 and x=−1. f'' = 6x−6. f''(3) = 12 > 0: local minimum, f(3) = 27−27−27+5 = −22. f''(−1) = −12 < 0: local maximum, f(−1) = −1−3+9+5 = 10.
  6. For all three, the derivatives vanish at 0: f'' = 12x², g'' = −12x², h'' = 6x, so each second derivative is 0 at x=0 and the test says nothing. First Derivative Test: f' = 4x³ is negative for x<0 and positive for x>0, so x⁴ has a local minimum; g' = −4x³ is positive then negative, so −x⁴ has a local maximum; h' = 3x² is positive on both sides, so x³ has neither (it is increasing through 0). One failed test, three different truths.
  7. f'' = −1/(4x^(3/2)) < 0 for x>0, so f is concave down near 4 and the tangent line lies above the graph: L(4.2) is an overestimate. L(4.2) = 2 + 0.2/4 = 2.0500; √4.2 ≈ 2.0494. The prediction holds (2.0500 > 2.0494).

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 23 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 23 Problem Set: Curve Sketching and Graph Analysis

Calculus Honors · Module 11. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. Intercepts: f = x(x−3)², so (0,0) and (3,0); y-intercept 0. f' = 3x²−12x+9 = 3(x−1)(x−3); f'' = 6x−12. Critical points x=1, 3. f''(1) = −6 < 0: local max (1, 4). f''(3) = 6 > 0: local min (3, 0) (also an x-intercept where the graph touches the axis). Inflection: f''=0 at x=2, sign change, f(2) = 2: (2, 2). End behavior: f → −∞ as x → −∞ and f → +∞ as x → +∞. Increasing on (−∞,1) and (3,∞), decreasing on (1,3); concave down on (−∞,2), concave up on (2,∞). The sketch rises through the origin to (1,4), falls through (2,2) to touch the axis at (3,0), then rises.
  2. f(−x) = −f(x): odd, symmetric about the origin. Denominator never 0, so the domain is all reals; as x → ±∞, f → 0, so horizontal asymptote y = 0. f' = 0 at x = ±1: f'>0 on (−1,1), f'<0 outside. Local min (−1, −1/2), local max (1, 1/2). f'' = 0 at x = 0 and x = ±√3; the sign chart of 2x(x²−3)/(x²+1)³ gives f''<0 on (−∞,−√3), >0 on (−√3,0), <0 on (0,√3), >0 on (√3,∞): concavity changes at all three, so three inflection points: x = −√3, 0, √3, at y = −√3/4, 0, √3/4.
  3. Vertical asymptote x = 1 (numerator is 1 there). Division: x²/(x−1) = x + 1 + 1/(x−1), so the slant asymptote is y = x + 1. f' = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2 (undefined only at the asymptote). f'>0 on (−∞,0), <0 on (0,1), <0 on (1,2), >0 on (2,∞): local max (0, 0), local min (2, 4). f'' = 2/(x−1)³: negative for x<1 (concave down), positive for x>1 (concave up). Concavity changes at x = 1, but f is not defined there, so there is no inflection point: an inflection point must be a point on the graph.
  4. For x ≠ 2: f' = −(2/3)(x−2)^(−1/3); f'' = (2/9)(x−2)^(−4/3) > 0. At x=2, f' is undefined: as x → 2⁻, f' → +∞; as x → 2⁺, f' → −∞. f' changes from + to −, so x = 2 is a local (and absolute) maximum, f(2) = 2, with a cusp (a sharp point with vertical tangent directions). f'' > 0 on both sides: concave up on (−∞,2) and (2,∞). The concavity does not change, so (2,2) is not an inflection point.
  5. Answers vary; the sketch must satisfy every condition. One function that works: f(x) = (x³ − 3x² − 9x + 11)/4. Required features: local max (−1, 4) (f' goes + to −), local min (3, −4) (f' goes − to +), inflection point (1, 0) (f'' goes − to +). The graph rises, concave down, to (−1,4); falls through (1,0) where it changes from concave down to concave up; bottoms out at (3,−4); then rises concave up.
  6. f' = −(x−1)(x−5). f'>0 on (1,5) (the parabola is above the axis there) and f'<0 outside. So f is decreasing on (−∞,1), increasing on (1,5), decreasing on (5,∞): local minimum at x=1 (f' from − to +), local maximum at x=5. Concavity comes from the slope of f': the parabola's vertex is at x = 3 (its maximum), so f' increases on (−∞,3) and decreases on (3,∞): f'' = −2x+6 is positive then negative. f is concave up on (−∞,3), concave down on (3,∞), with an inflection point at x = 3.
  7. (a) False. f(x) = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but f'' = 12x² does not change sign: no inflection point. (b) False. f(x) = −|x| has a local (absolute) maximum at 0, but f'(0) does not exist (it is a corner). A local extremum happens at a critical point: f' = 0 or undefined. (c) True: this is the Second Derivative Test. f'(c)=0 says the tangent is horizontal and f''(c)>0 says the graph is concave up there, so it sits above its horizontal tangent: a local minimum.

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 11 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 11 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 11. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. Since f'' > 0 on I, f' is increasing on I: for u < v in I, the MVT applied to f' (differentiable, hence continuous, on [u,v]) gives f'(v) − f'(u) = f''(ξ)(v−u) > 0. Now fix c and x in I with x > c. The MVT applied to f on [c,x] (continuous on [c,x], differentiable on (c,x)) gives ξ∈(c,x) with f(x) − f(c) = f'(ξ)(x−c). Since ξ > c and f' is increasing, f'(ξ) > f'(c), and x−c > 0, so f(x) − f(c) > f'(c)(x−c), that is, f(x) > f(c) + f'(c)(x−c). If x < c, apply the MVT on [x,c]: f(c)−f(x) = f'(ξ)(c−x) with ξ < c, so f'(ξ) < f'(c) and f(c) − f(x) < f'(c)(c−x), which rearranges to the same inequality. Conclusion: when f''>0, every tangent-line (linear) approximation underestimates f (and when f''<0 it overestimates). Look for: MVT used twice with hypotheses named, both cases x>c and x<c, and the connection to Lesson 9.03.

Part B. f(x) = x²/(x²−1) = 1 + 1/(x²−1). Domain: x ≠ ±1. Intercept: (0,0) only (numerator zero only at 0). Symmetry: f(−x) = f(x): even, symmetric about the y-axis. Asymptotes: vertical x = 1 and x = −1 (denominator 0, numerator 1); horizontal y = 1 (f → 1 as x → ±∞). Since f − 1 = 1/(x²−1), which is positive for |x|>1 and negative for |x|<1, the graph approaches y=1 from above as x → ±∞. f': by the Quotient Rule (or d/dx[1+(x²−1)⁻¹] = −(x²−1)⁻²·2x) f' = −2x/(x²−1)². Only critical number in the domain: x = 0, with f(0) = 0. f'>0 for x<0 (x≠−1) and f'<0 for x>0 (x≠1): increasing on (−∞,−1) and (−1,0); decreasing on (0,1) and (1,∞). Local maximum at (0,0). f'': f'' = (6x²+2)/(x²−1)³. The numerator is always positive, so the sign is that of (x²−1)³: f''>0 for |x|>1 (concave up on (−∞,−1) and (1,∞)), f''<0 for |x|<1 (concave down on (−1,1)). The concavity changes only at ±1, which are not in the domain: no inflection points. (Check at the max: f''(0) = 2/(−1)³ = −2 < 0, consistent with a local max.) Sketch: two branches above y=1 outside the asymptotes, each rising to +∞ at the asymptote and flattening toward y=1; between the asymptotes, a downward cap through (0,0) falling to −∞ at x=±1.

Part C. f' = 3ax²+2bx+c. Conditions: f(0)=5 ⇒ d=5; f'(0)=0 ⇒ c=0; f'(2)=0 ⇒ 12a+4b=0; f(2)=1 ⇒ 8a+4b+5=1 ⇒ 8a+4b=−4. Subtract: 4a = 4 ⇒ a=1, then b=−3. f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 5. Check: f' = 3x(x−2), f(2) = 8−12+5 = 1 ✓; f'' = 6x−6, zero at x=1 with a sign change: inflection point (1, 3), and 1 is the midpoint of 0 and 2. Why always: for a cubic, f' = 3a(x−r₁)(x−r₂) is a parabola, symmetric about its vertex at x = (r₁+r₂)/2; f'' = (f')' is zero exactly at the vertex and changes sign there, so the inflection point is the midpoint of the critical numbers.

Part D. For x ≠ 0: f' = (1/3)x^(−2/3) > 0 (increasing; vertical tangent at 0, where f' is undefined); f'' = −(2/9)x^(−5/3). For x<0, x^(−5/3) < 0, so f'' > 0 (concave up); for x>0, f'' < 0 (concave down). f is continuous at 0 and the concavity changes there, so (0,0) is an inflection point although f''(0) does not exist (not necessary). Conversely, f(x) = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but f'' = 12x² ≥ 0 never changes sign, so there is no inflection point (not sufficient). The definition requires: the graph has a tangent line (possibly vertical) at the point, and the concavity changes from one side to the other. Full credit for stating that the sign change, not the value of f'', is what matters; that a zero or an undefined f'' only marks a candidate.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct derivatives, asymptotes, classification, and the cubic's coefficients.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): Part A uses the MVT twice with hypotheses checked and handles both x>c and x<c; Part B argues concavity from the sign of each factor; Part D separates "candidate" from "inflection point."
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, exact values, a large, labeled sketch.
  • Intellectual honesty (4): states what is proven versus only checked, and says plainly that f'' = 0 is not enough.

ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 27 Problem Set: Riemann Sums

Calculus Honors · Module 13. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. Width Δx = 1. Left uses f(0),f(1),f(2),f(3) = 1,2,5,10, so L = 18. Right uses f(1..4) = 2,5,10,17, so R = 34. Midpoint uses x = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5: f = 1.25, 3.25, 7.25, 13.25, so M = 25. f is increasing on [0,4], so each left rectangle sits under the curve (underestimate) and each right rectangle pokes above it (overestimate); the midpoint rectangle is in between. (Exact area is 76/3 ≈ 25.33: left too low, right too high, midpoint very close.)
  2. Left sum = 1·(30+22+15+9) = 76 ft; right sum = 1·(22+15+9+4) = 50 ft. The speed is decreasing the whole time, so on each second the car was never faster than at the start of that second (left sum is an upper bound) and never slower than at the end (right sum is a lower bound): the distance is between 50 and 76 ft. A single best estimate is the average, 63 ft. Accept any answer that explains the bound with monotonicity.
  3. Left = 1(1+1/2+1/3+1/4) = 25/12 ≈ 2.083; right = 1(1/2+1/3+1/4+1/5) = 77/60 ≈ 1.283. f(x)=1/x is decreasing, so left is an overestimate and right is an underestimate. Check: 1.283 < 1.609 < 2.083 ✓.
  4. Sum = 1+3+5+7+9 = 25. Sigma form: Σ_{k=1}^{10} 3k (equivalently 3Σk). Σ_{k=1}^{10} k² = 10·11·21/6 = 385.
  5. Δx = 3/n, x_k = 3k/n. R_n = Σ_{k=1}^{n} (3k/n)²(3/n) = (27/n³)Σk² = (27/n³)·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = 9(n+1)(2n+1)/(2n²). As n→∞ this is 9·(2n²)/(2n²) → 9 (equivalently 9(1+1/n)(2+1/n)/2 → 9·2/2).
  6. Δx = 4/n, left endpoints x_{k−1} = 4(k−1)/n. L_n = Σ_{k=1}^{n}[8(k−1)/n + 1](4/n) = (4/n)[(8/n)·n(n−1)/2 + n] = (4/n)(5n−4) = 20 − 16/n → 20. Geometry: trapezoid with parallel sides f(0)=1 and f(4)=9 and width 4: (1+9)/2·4 = 20 ✓.
  7. For f(x)=x on [0,2]: midpoint with n=1 uses f(1)=1 times width 2, giving 2, which is exactly the area (a triangle: ½·2·2). Left with n=4: 0.5(0+0.5+1+1.5) = 1.5. So the claim is false for this example. The example shows that the midpoint rule can be far more accurate than the left rule for the same or fewer rectangles (midpoint errors for a linear function cancel). It does not show midpoint is always better; it shows only that "more rectangles" is not the whole story, and that the rule matters as much as n.

ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 28 Problem Set: The Definite Integral and the Trapezoidal Rule

Calculus Honors · Module 13. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. (a) The graph is the upper half of a circle of radius 3: area = ½·π·3² = 9π/2. (b) f(x)=x−1 is below the axis on [−1,1] (triangle, base 2, height 2, area 2, counts −2) and above it on [1,3] (triangle area 2, counts +2): total 0. (c) Two triangles each with base 2 and height 2, both above the axis: 2+2 = 4.
  2. (a) Additivity: 3 + (−1) = 2. (b) Reversing limits: −∫₀⁵ f = −2. (c) Linearity: 2(2) − 3(4) = −8.
  3. Take Δx = 2/n, so b−a = 2; sample points x_k = 1 + 2k/n = a + kΔx with a = 1, so b = 3 and f(x) = √x. The limit is ∫₁³ √x dx.
  4. For 0≤x≤1, 0≤x²≤1, so −1≤−x²≤0, and since eˣ is increasing, e⁻¹ ≤ e^{−x²} ≤ e⁰ = 1. Comparison property (and the integral of a constant over an interval of length 1): e⁻¹ ≤ ∫₀¹ e^{−x²}dx ≤ 1, i.e. about 0.368 ≤ I ≤ 1. To narrow it, split [0,1] into pieces and bound the function on each piece (equivalently, use left and right sums, since e^{−x²} is decreasing on [0,1]).

  6. L₄ = 2+3+5+8 = 18; R₄ = 3+5+8+12 = 28; T₄ = ½[2 + 2(3+5+8) + 12] = 23. (L+R)/2 = 23 ✓. Reason: the area of each trapezoid is the average of the left rectangle and the right rectangle on that subinterval; summing gives the average of the two sums.

Midpoints 1/4, 3/4, 5/4, 7/4 give f = 1/16, 9/16, 25/16, 49/16 and M₄ = (1/2)(84/16) = 21/8 = 2.625. Exact = 8/3 ≈ 2.667. T₄ is an overestimate (error +1/12) and M₄ an underestimate (error −1/24). f is concave up (f″ = 2 > 0): a chord lies above a concave-up curve (trapezoid too big), while the tangent at the midpoint lies below it (midpoint too small). pages.title: Answer Key - Module 13 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 13 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 13. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. Δx = b/n, x_k = kb/n. R_n = Σ_{k=1}^{n}(kb/n)²(b/n) = (b³/n³)Σk² = (b³/n³)·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = b³(n+1)(2n+1)/(6n²), using Σk² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. Then R_n = (b³/6)(1+1/n)(2+1/n) → (b³/6)(2) = b³/3. So ∫₀ᵇ x²dx = b³/3. Look for: Δx and x_k stated, the summation formula named, the limit justified by 1/n → 0.

Part B. (i) Linearity: ∫₀³(2x²+1)dx = 2∫₀³x²dx + ∫₀³1 dx = 2(9) + 3 = 21 (using Part A with b=3 gives 27/3 = 9, and the rectangle of height 1 and width 3). (ii) Additivity: ∫₁³x² = ∫₀³x² − ∫₀¹x² = 9 − 1/3 = 26/3 (Part A with b=1 gives 1/3).

Part C. Δx = 1/2; x = 1, 3/2, 2, 5/2, 3; f = 1, 2/3, 1/2, 2/5, 1/3. T₄ = (1/4)[1 + 2(2/3+1/2+2/5) + 1/3] = (1/4)(67/15) = 67/60 ≈ 1.1167. Midpoints 5/4, 7/4, 9/4, 11/4: f = 0.8, 0.5714, 0.4444, 0.3636, and M₄ = (1/2)(2.1795) ≈ 1.0898. ln 3 ≈ 1.0986. So T₄ overestimates (error ≈ +0.0181) and M₄ underestimates (error ≈ −0.0088). f''(x) = 2/x³ > 0 on [1,3], so f is concave up: chords lie above the curve (trapezoids too big) and tangent lines lie below it (midpoint too small). The trapezoid error is about twice the midpoint error in size.

Part D. No. The computer value 9.0000135 equals 9(n+1)(2n+1)/(2n²) at n = 10⁶ exactly, so it shows the sums are very close to 9 and still above it; it does not show the area is exactly 9 (a different function could produce the same digits), and it checks one n only. The Part A limit shows that the sums approach 9 as n grows without bound, which is exact. What both assume: the limit argument assumes the Riemann sums settle on a single number that deserves to be called the area (true here because f is continuous, as the next lesson's integrability result guarantees); the computer assumes its arithmetic is correct and that one large n is representative. Full credit for separating "close" from "exactly equal" and for naming the limit as the exact statement.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct closed form, limit, property use, T₄ and M₄ values.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): summation formula stated; properties named; over/under claims tied to concavity; Part D distinguishes estimate from limit.
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, exact fractions, labeled answers.
  • Intellectual honesty (4): says what is proven versus checked; names the assumption behind the limit.

ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 29 Problem Set: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

Calculus Honors · Module 14. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. Part 1: F'(x) = x²+1 (the integrand evaluated at x). Part 2: F(x) = [t³/3 + t] from 1 to x = (x³/3 + x) − (1/3 + 1) = x³/3 + x − 4/3. Differentiating gives x²+1, so both methods agree.
  2. g'(x) = √(x³+1), so g'(3) = √28 = 2√7. Part 1 says the derivative of an accumulation function is the integrand, so no formula for g is needed (here √(t³+1) has no elementary antiderivative at all).
  3. (a) Chain Rule on the upper limit: d/dx ∫₁^{x²} ln t dt = ln(x²)·(2x) = 2 ln x · 2x = 4x ln x (x>0). (b) The variable is the lower limit: flip the limits first, ∫ₓ⁵ = −∫₅ˣ, so the derivative is −e^{x²}.
  4. (a) [x³ − x² + x]₀² = 8 − 4 + 2 = 6. (b) [(2/3)x^{3/2}]₁⁴ = (2/3)(8) − (2/3)(1) = 14/3. (c) [sin x]₀^{π/2} = 1 − 0 = 1.
  5. ∫(x−1)dx = [x²/2 − x] from −1 to 2 = (2−2) − (1/2+1) = −3/2. The line is below the axis on [−1,1) and above on (1,2]. Area = ∫₋₁¹(1−x)dx + ∫₁²(x−1)dx = 2 + 1/2 = 5/2. The integral is signed: the region below the axis counts negatively (−2 + 1/2 = −3/2), while area counts every region positively.
  6. F(2) = triangle area (1/2)(2)(2) = 2. F(4) = 2 + 2 = 4. From 4 to 6 the graph is below the axis: a triangle of area 2 counts −2, so F(6) = 2. F'(x) = f(x), so F increases where f>0, i.e., on (0,4), and decreases on (4,6). The largest value is F(4) = 4, at x = 4 where f changes from positive to negative.
  7. G'(x) = f(x) by Part 1 and F'(x) = f(x) by hypothesis, so (G−F)' = 0 on [a,b]. A function with zero derivative on an interval is constant (a consequence of the Mean Value Theorem, Lesson 8.04), so G(x) − F(x) = C. At x = a: G(a) = 0, so C = −F(a). Then at x = b: G(b) = F(b) + C = F(b) − F(a), and G(b) = ∫ₐᵇ f. ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a).

F(x) = x³/3 − x² − 3x, so F(0) = 0, F(3) = 9 − 9 − 9 = −9, F(5) = 125/3 − 25 − 15 = 5/3. Absolute max 5/3 at x = 5; absolute min −9 at x = 3.
  4. (a) u = x²+1, du = 2x dx: ∫u⁵du = u⁶/6 + C = (x²+1)⁶/6 + C. (b) u = x³, du = 3x²dx: (1/3)∫cos u du = (1/3) sin(x³) + C. (c) u = 3x: (1/3)e^{3x} + C. Each is checked by differentiating (Chain Rule).
  5. (a) u = x², du = 2x dx; limits 0→0, 1→1: (1/2)∫₀¹ e^u du = (e−1)/2. (b) u = cos x, du = −sin x dx; limits π/2 ⇒ 0, 0 ⇒ 1: −∫₁⁰ u² du = ∫₀¹ u² du = 1/3.
  6. With u = x²+16, du = 2x dx; x=0 gives u=16, x=3 gives u=25: (1/2)∫₁₆²⁵ u^{−1/2} du = [√u] = 5 − 4 = 1. In x: antiderivative √(x²+16), so √25 − √16 = 1. They agree.
  7. u = x² needs the factor du = 2x dx to appear in the integrand: xe^{x²} contains it (up to the constant 1/2), but e^{x²} alone does not, and no other choice of u works. By Part 1, since e^{t²} is continuous, F(x) = ∫₀ˣ e^{t²} dt satisfies F' = e^{x²}. So an antiderivative exists even though it has no formula in elementary functions. Look for the distinction between having an antiderivative and being able to write one.

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 14 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 14 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 14. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. For h>0, G(x+h) − G(x) = ∫ₓ^{x+h} f(t) dt (additivity of the integral). Since f is continuous on the closed interval [x,x+h], the Extreme Value Theorem gives a minimum m_h and a maximum M_h of f there, and m_h·h ≤ ∫ₓ^{x+h} f ≤ M_h·h (comparison property). Divide by h>0: m_h ≤ [G(x+h)−G(x)]/h ≤ M_h. As h→0⁺, continuity of f at x forces both m_h and M_h to approach f(x) (every value of f on [x,x+h] is within ε of f(x) for small h). By the Squeeze Theorem the difference quotient tends to f(x). For h<0 the same argument works on [x+h,x] (the quotient is still the average of f over an interval ending at x). So G'(x) = f(x). Continuity is used in two places: EVT on the small interval, and m_h, M_h → f(x). Look for the names of EVT, the comparison property, and the Squeeze Theorem.

Part B. (i) ∫₀⁶ (6−2t) dt = [6t − t²]₀⁶ = 36 − 36 = 0 gal. (ii) V(t) = 50 + ∫₀ᵗ (6−2s) ds = 50 + 6t − t²; V(3) = 50 + 18 − 9 = 59 gal. (iii) V' = r = 6−2t is positive before t=3 and negative after, so V rises then falls: V''(t) = −2 < 0 (or the sign change of V') gives a maximum at t = 3 min, V = 59 gal. (iv) V(0) = V(6) = 50, and V is a downward parabola, so the least volume on [0,6] is 50 gal, attained at both endpoints (closed-interval method). For h(x): write h(x) = H(x²) − H(x) with H' = sin(t²); then h'(x) = 2x sin(x⁴) − sin(x²) (Part 1 + Chain Rule on the upper limit, minus the lower-limit term).

Part C. (a) u = tan x, du = sec²x dx; limits 0→0, π/4→1: ∫₀¹ u du = 1/2. (b) u = ln x, du = dx/x; limits 1→0, e→1: ∫₀¹ u² du = 1/3. Wrong version: with u = x²+1, ∫ u³ du = u⁴/4, but keeping 0 and 1 as u-limits gives [u⁴/4]₀¹ = 1/4, which is wrong. Correct: u runs from 1 to 2, giving (16 − 1)/4 = 15/4 (check: [(x²+1)⁴/4]₀¹ = 15/4). The limits belong to x; after substituting they must become limits on u, or you must return to x before evaluating.

Part D. F'(x) = e^{−x²} > 0 for all x (Part 1), so F is increasing. F''(x) = −2x e^{−x²} < 0 for x>0, so F is concave down on (0,∞). On [0,1], 1 − t² ≤ e^{−t²} ≤ 1 (the left side from e^{u} ≥ 1+u with u = −t²). Integrating (comparison property): ∫₀¹(1−t²)dt = 2/3 ≤ F(1) ≤ ∫₀¹ 1 dt = 1. 2/3 ≤ F(1) ≤ 1 is proved; the actual value (≈ 0.7468) is only bounded here, not found. We "know" F in the sense that it is a well-defined function with a known derivative, a known graph shape, and values we can compute to any accuracy by Riemann sums or the Trapezoidal Rule, even without a closed form. Full credit for separating "an antiderivative exists" (Part 1 guarantees it) from "a formula exists" (it does not), and for labeling the bound as a bound.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct accumulation-function derivative, net change values, substitution results, and bounds.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): Part A proof names EVT, comparison, and Squeeze and says where continuity enters; Part C explains why the limits must change.
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, exact values, labeled answers, units (gallons, minutes).
  • Intellectual honesty (4): distinguishes proved bounds from the unknown exact value; candid about uncertainty.

ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 31 Problem Set: Antiderivatives and Slope Fields

Calculus Honors · Module 15. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. ∫(6x²−4x+5)dx = 2x³ − 2x² + 5x + C. Check: d/dx = 6x² − 4x + 5 ✓.
  2. 5 sin x − 2eˣ + ln x + C (ln|x| in general; x>0 here). Check: 5cos x − 2eˣ + 1/x ✓.
  3. f(x) = 2x³ − x² + C. f(1) = 2−1+C = 1 + C = 4, so C = 3. f(x) = 2x³ − x² + 3.
  4. f'(x) = 6x² − 6x + C₁. f'(1) = 6−6+C₁ = C₁ = 5. So f'(x) = 6x²−6x+5. Then f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + 5x + C₂, and f(0) = C₂ = 2. f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + 5x + 2. Check: f'' = 12x−6 ✓. Each integration brings one constant, and each condition fixes one.
  5. v(t) = 3t² − 4t + C₁ and v(0) = 3 gives v(t) = 3t² − 4t + 3. s(t) = t³ − 2t² + 3t + C₂ and s(0) = 1 gives s(t) = t³ − 2t² + 3t + 1. v(2) = 12−8+3 = 7 m/s; s(2) = 8−8+6+1 = 7 m. Units on every answer.
  6. Slope = x − y. Rows y = 1, 0, −1 and columns x = −1, 0, 1: y=1: −2, −1, 0; y=0: −1, 0, 1; y=−1: 0, 1, 2. Verify: y = x−1 gives y' = 1 and x−y = x−(x−1) = 1 ✓. Along that line every segment has slope 1, the same slope as the line itself, so the segments lie along the line: a solution curve follows the slope field. (Full credit for noting that points on the line y = x−1 all have slope 1.)
  7. (a) Slope = y depends only on y: along the x-axis (y=0) the segments are horizontal; along any horizontal line the segments are all parallel; along the y-axis the slope equals the height y. (b) Slope = x depends only on x: along the y-axis (x=0) the segments are horizontal; along any vertical line the segments are all parallel; along the x-axis the slope equals x. (c) Slope = xy is zero on both axes, so all segments are horizontal on both axes; positive in quadrants I and III, negative in II and IV.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 32 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 32 Problem Set: Separable Equations and Growth and Decay

Calculus Honors · Module 15. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. Separate: dy/y = 2x dx (y≠0). Integrate: ln|y| = x² + C. So y = Ke^(x²). y(0) = K = 3. y = 3e^(x²). Check: y' = 6xe^(x²) = 2x·y ✓ and y(0) = 3 ✓.
  2. Separate: y dy = x dx. Integrate: y²/2 = x²/2 + C, so y² = x² + C'. y(0) = 2 gives C' = 4. y² = x²+4, and since y(0) = 2 > 0 we take the positive root: y = √(x²+4). Check: y' = x/√(x²+4) = x/y ✓.
  3. dy/y² = dx gives −1/y = x + C. y(0)=1: −1 = C. So −1/y = x−1, y = 1/(1−x). Valid on the interval x < 1 (it contains x=0). As x→1⁻, y→+∞: the solution blows up in finite time, so it cannot be extended past x = 1. y = 0 is a solution (0 = 0²). Separation divided by y², which is illegal at y = 0, so that constant solution was lost.
  4. dy/(y−1) = 2 dx gives ln|y−1| = 2x + C, so y−1 = Ke^(2x). y(0)=3: K = 2. y = 1 + 2e^(2x). Check: y' = 4e^(2x) = 2(y−1) ✓. Dividing by y−1 lost the constant solution y = 1 (it makes dy/dx = 0 = 2(1−1)). It is selected by y(0) = 1 (K = 0).
  5. dP/P = 0.03 dt gives P = 500e^(0.03t). P(10) = 500e^(0.3) ≈ 674.9. Doubling: e^(0.03T) = 2, T = ln 2 / 0.03 ≈ 23.1 years. Note the doubling time does not depend on P(0).
  6. Half-life: e^(5730k) = 1/2, so k = −ln 2 / 5730 ≈ −1.2097×10⁻⁴ per year. A(t) = A₀e^(−t ln2/5730) = A₀·2^(−t/5730). At t = 10{,}000: 2^(−10000/5730) ≈ 0.2983, about 29.8%.
  7. P(100) = 500e³ ≈ 10{,}043. Look for an honest judgment: the model assumes a constant per-capita growth rate forever, so it ignores limited food, space, competition, disease, and changing birth and death rates; it is trustworthy only while the population is far below such limits. (Full credit for naming at least one omitted factor and saying the prediction is an extrapolation.)

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 15 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 15 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 15. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. g'(t) = y'(t)e^(−kt) + y(t)·(−k)e^(−kt) = e^(−kt)(y' − ky) = 0. A function whose derivative is 0 on an interval is constant (Lesson 8.04, a consequence of the Mean Value Theorem), so g(t) = g(0) = y(0). Then y(t)e^(−kt) = y(0), so y(t) = y(0)e^(kt). If y(0) = 0 this gives y ≡ 0, so the constant solution is included automatically: nothing was divided by y, so nothing was lost. Look for: the product and chain rule done correctly, the invocation of the zero-derivative theorem by name, and the observation that this proof never divides by y.

Part B. u = T−20, so du/dt = dT/dt = −k(T−20) = −ku: a decay equation, u = u₀e^(−kt). u(0) = 90−20 = 70, so u = 70e^(−kt). At t = 10, T = 60 gives u = 40: 70e^(−10k) = 40, e^(−10k) = 4/7, k = (1/10) ln(7/4) ≈ 0.05596 per minute. For T = 30, u = 10: e^(−kt) = 1/7, so kt = ln 7 and t = ln 7 / k = 10 ln 7 / ln(7/4) ≈ 34.77 minutes. Check: 70e^(−k·34.77) = 70/7 = 10 ✓.

Part C. Separating (y≠0): −1/y = x + C. y(0)=1: C = −1, y = 1/(1−x), valid on x < 1. y(0)=−1: −1/y = x + C with −1/(−1) = 1 = C, so −1/y = x+1 and y = −1/(x+1), valid on x > −1. y(0)=0: separation divides by y², so it cannot find it; check directly that y = 0 works, valid for all x. For y(0)=1: y(0.9) = 1/0.1 = 10, y(0.99) = 100, while e^0.9 ≈ 2.46. The solution of y' = y² explodes at x = 1 because the growth rate itself grows with y², faster than with y. A model that blows up in finite time has stopped describing reality before the blow-up: some factor it leaves out (limited resources, saturation) must matter well before the infinite value.

Part D. 2^(−t/5730) = 0.3, so t = 5730·log₂(10/3) = 5730 ln(10/3) / ln 2 ≈ 9953 years. Differential: with N the remaining fraction, t = (5730/ln 2)·(−ln N), so dt = −(5730/ln 2)(dN/N). With N = 0.3 and dN = ±0.01: |dt| = (5730/ln 2)(0.01/0.3) ≈ 276 years. Exact: 29% gives ≈ 10{,}233 years, 31% gives ≈ 9682 years, so the age ranges from 9682 to 10{,}233: ≈ +280 and ≈ −271 years from 9953, and the differential's 276 sits between them. Assumptions to expect: the decay rate is constant and known, the sample started with the standard ratio of carbon-14 and was a closed system, and the measurement of 30% is accurate. The estimate promises a reasonable range under those assumptions; it does not promise the true age if an assumption fails.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct solutions to each differential equation, correct use of initial conditions, exact and decimal values.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): Part A uses the zero-derivative theorem rather than separation; Part C finds the lost solution and the domains; Part D justifies the differential.
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, exact values (logarithms) before decimals, units and intervals stated, labeled answers.
  • Intellectual honesty (4): names the assumptions of each model (constant rate, closed sample, Newton's law) and what the estimates do not guarantee.

ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 33 Problem Set: Area and Average Value

Calculus Honors · Module 16. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. x² = 6 − x ⇒ x² + x − 6 = 0 ⇒ (x+3)(x−2) = 0 ⇒ x = −3, 2. On [−3,2] the line is above the parabola. Area = ∫₋₃² (6 − x − x²) dx = [6x − x²/2 − x³/3]₋₃² = (12 − 2 − 8/3) − (−18 − 9/2 + 9) = 22/3 − (−27/2) = 125/6.
  2. x³ = 4x ⇒ x(x−2)(x+2) = 0 ⇒ x = −2, 0, 2. On [−2,0], x³ ≥ 4x (top is x³); on [0,2], 4x ≥ x³ (top is 4x). One integral of x³−4x over [−2,2] gives the signed total, 0 by symmetry, because the two pieces cancel. Area = ∫₋₂⁰ (x³−4x) dx + ∫₀² (4x−x³) dx = 4 + 4 = 8 (each piece is [2x² − x⁴/4] = 8 − 4 = 4).
  3. sin x = cos x at x = π/4. On [0,π/4], cos ≥ sin; on [π/4,π/2], sin ≥ cos. Area = [sin x + cos x]₀^(π/4) + [−cos x − sin x]_(π/4)^(π/2) = (√2 − 1) + (−1 + √2) = 2√2 − 2 = 2(√2−1) ≈ 0.828.
  4. Intersection: √x = x − 6 ⇒ x = 9 (x = 4 is extraneous: √4 = 2 ≠ −2), the point (9,3). In terms of y: x = y² (left) and x = y + 6 (right) for 0 ≤ y ≤ 3. Area = ∫₀³ (y + 6 − y²) dy = [y²/2 + 6y − y³/3]₀³ = 9/2 + 18 − 9 = 27/2. With respect to x the lower boundary changes from the x-axis (0 ≤ x ≤ 6) to the line y = x−6 (6 ≤ x ≤ 9): two integrals, ∫₀⁶ √x dx + ∫₆⁹ (√x − x + 6) dx, giving the same 27/2.
  5. Average = (1/2)∫₀² x³ dx = (1/2)(4) = 2. f(c) = c³ = 2 ⇒ c = ∛2 ≈ 1.260 (in [0,2]). The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals guarantees such a c for any continuous function on a closed interval.
  6. Average = (1/(e−1))∫₁ᵉ (1/x) dx = (1/(e−1))[ln x]₁ᵉ = (1/(e−1))(1 − 0) = 1/(e−1) ≈ 0.582. Geometrically: the rectangle on [1,e] with height 1/(e−1) has the same area (1) as the region under y = 1/x on [1,e].
  7. v = (t−2)(t−4). ∫₀⁵ v dt = [t³/3 − 3t² + 8t]₀⁵ = 125/3 − 75 + 40 = 20/3 (by pieces: 20/3 − 4/3 + 4/3), so average velocity = (20/3)/5 = 4/3 m/s. Speed uses |v|: ∫₀² v = 20/3 (forward), ∫₂⁴ (−v) = 4/3 (backward), ∫₄⁵ v = 4/3 (forward). Total distance = 20/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 28/3 m, so average speed = (28/3)/5 = 28/15 m/s. They differ because velocity is signed: the backward motion on [2,4] cancels part of the forward motion in the average velocity, but speed counts all the distance traveled.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 34 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 34 Problem Set: Volumes

Calculus Honors · Module 16. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. Side = √x, so A(x) = (√x)² = x. V = ∫₀⁴ x dx = [x²/2]₀⁴ = 8.
  2. Intersections: x = x³ ⇒ x = 0, 1; on (0,1) the line is on top. Diameter d(x) = x − x³, radius d/2. A(x) = (π/2)(d/2)² = (π/8)(x−x³)². V = (π/8)∫₀¹ (x² − 2x⁴ + x⁶) dx = (π/8)(1/3 − 2/5 + 1/7) = (π/8)(8/105) = π/105.
  3. The chord at x has length s = 2√(1−x²), so A(x) = (√3/4)s² = (√3/4)(4)(1−x²) = √3(1−x²). V = √3 ∫₋₁¹ (1−x²) dx = √3 (4/3) = 4√3/3 ≈ 2.309.
  4. Disk radius = √x, A(x) = π(√x)² = πx. V = π ∫₀⁴ x dx = π(8) = 8π ≈ 25.13.
  5. Solve y = x² for x: radius = √y (x ≥ 0), for 0 ≤ y ≤ 4. V = π ∫₀⁴ (√y)² dy = π ∫₀⁴ y dy = π(8) = 8π. (Slices are perpendicular to the y-axis, so everything is in terms of y.)
  6. √x = x² ⇒ x = 0, 1; on (0,1), √x ≥ x². Outer radius √x, inner radius x². V = π∫₀¹ ((√x)² − (x²)²) dx = π∫₀¹ (x − x⁴) dx = π(1/2 − 1/5) = 3π/10. The washer's area is the area of the big disk minus the area of the hole, πR² − πr², a difference of squares, not π(R−r)².
  7. Rotating about y = −1, the distance from the axis to the curve is outer R = x² + 1, and to the x-axis (the region's lower edge) is inner r = 1. V = π∫₀¹ ((x²+1)² − 1²) dx = π∫₀¹ (x⁴ + 2x²) dx = π(1/5 + 2/3) = 13π/15. Each radius is measured from the axis of rotation, which is why the 1 appears in both.

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 16 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 16 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 16. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. f is continuous on the closed interval [a,b], so by the Extreme Value Theorem it has an absolute minimum m and an absolute maximum M on [a,b] (hypothesis: continuity on a closed interval). Since m ≤ f(x) ≤ M, integrating gives m(b−a) ≤ ∫ₐᵇ f ≤ M(b−a), so m ≤ f_avg ≤ M. The minimum and maximum are attained at points of [a,b], and f is continuous, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem f takes every value between m and M, in particular f_avg, at some c in [a,b]. Check with f(x) = x² on [1,3]: ∫₁³ x² dx = 26/3, f_avg = (1/2)(26/3) = 13/3; c² = 13/3 ⇒ c = √(13/3) ≈ 2.082, which lies in [1,3] ✓. Look for: EVT and IVT both named, the inequality chain, continuity checked as a hypothesis.

Part B. x² = 2x ⇒ x = 0, 2; the line y = 2x is on top. (i) Area = ∫₀² (2x−x²) dx = [x² − x³/3]₀² = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3. (ii) The vertical distance is g(x) = 2x−x²; its average on [0,2] is (1/2)(4/3) = 2/3. (iii) Washers about the x-axis: outer R = 2x, inner r = x². V = π∫₀² ((2x)² − (x²)²) dx = π∫₀² (4x² − x⁴) dx = π(32/3 − 32/5) = 64π/15 ≈ 13.40.

Part C. (i) Radius of the disk at x is √(r²−x²), so A(x) = π(r²−x²) and V = π∫ from −r to r of (r²−x²) dx = π[r²x − x³/3] from −r to r = π(2r³ − 2r³/3) = 4πr³/3. (ii) By similar triangles the side at position x is 6x/9 = 2x/3, so A(x) = (2x/3)² = 4x²/9. V = ∫₀⁹ (4x²/9) dx = (4/9)(729/3) = 108. Check: this equals one third of base area times height, (1/3)(36)(9) = 108 ✓.

Part D. The classmate's number is π∫₀² (2x−x²)² dx = π∫₀² (4x² − 4x³ + x⁴) dx = π(32/3 − 16 + 32/5) = 16π/15, far from 64π/15. That integral is the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region under the single curve y = 2x−x² (the gap between the two curves, moved down onto the axis) about the x-axis: disks whose radius is the gap, not the washer-shaped solid in the problem. The washer's cross-section is a big disk minus a hole, πR² − πr² = π(R²−r²), and R²−r² = (R−r)(R+r) ≠ (R−r)²: areas subtract, radii do not. Slice summary: area, a thin rectangle of height (top − bottom); average value, the area divided by the width (the height of the rectangle with the same area); volume, a thin slab of known cross-sectional area A(x). Full credit for an honest statement of the weakest setup (for example, choosing the radius measured from an axis that is not the x-axis).

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct areas, average value, and volumes, with exact values.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): Part A names EVT and IVT and checks hypotheses; Part D explains difference of squares versus square of difference.
  • Clarity and precision (4): clean vertical work, labeled slices and radii, exact values (multiples of π), correct integrals with limits.
  • Intellectual honesty (4): candid about the weakest setup; separates what was proved from what was computed.

pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Semester 2 Review Activity (20 pts)

Calculus Honors · Semester 2 Finals Week. Do not distribute. Part 1 = 10 pts (completion and good-faith reasoning), Part 2 = 10 pts (all twelve rows present with a worked example each).

  1. f'(x) = 1/(2√x), f'(9) = 1/6, f(9) = 3. L(x) = 3 + (x−9)/6. L(9.2) = 3 + 0.2/6 = 91/30 ≈ 3.0333. √x is concave down (f'' = −¼x^(−3/2) < 0), so the tangent line lies above the curve: the estimate is too high (true √9.2 ≈ 3.03315).
  2. f' = 3x²−12x+9 = 3(x−1)(x−3). f' > 0 on (−∞,1), < 0 on (1,3), > 0 on (3,∞). Local max at x=1 (f=5), local min at x=3 (f=1). On [0,4]: f(0)=1, f(1)=5, f(3)=1, f(4)=5. Absolute max 5 (at x=1 and x=4); absolute min 1 (at x=0 and x=3).
  3. g'' = 12x²−24x = 12x(x−2). g'' > 0 on (−∞,0) and (2,∞); g'' < 0 on (0,2). Concavity changes at both zeros, so inflection points (0,0) and (2,−16). Concave up on (−∞,0)∪(2,∞); concave down on (0,2).
  4. Let the two sides perpendicular to the river be w, the side along it 200−2w. A = w(200−2w), 0 ≤ w ≤ 100. A' = 200−4w = 0 at w = 50. A(0)=0, A(100)=0, A(50)=5000. 50 m by 100 m, area 5000 m², the maximum by the Closed Interval Method (or A'' = −4 < 0).
  5. x²+y² = 169. At x=12, y=5. Differentiate: 2x·x' + 2y·y' = 0, so y' = −(x/y)x' = −(12/5)(2) = −24/5 ft/s = −4.8 ft/s (the top is sliding down at 4.8 ft/s).
  6. Δx = 0.5; right endpoints 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2: (0.25+1+2.25+4)(0.5) = 3.75. Exact: ∫₀²x²dx = 8/3 ≈ 2.667. Since x² is increasing on [0,2], right sums overestimate.
  7. (a) FTC Part 1 with the Chain Rule: 2x cos(x²). (b) ∫3√x dx = 2x^(3/2); [2x^(3/2)] from 1 to 4 = 2(8) − 2(1) = 14.
  8. u = x², du = 2x dx; x=0 → u=0, x=1 → u=1. ∫₀¹ e^u du = e − 1 = e−1 ≈ 1.718.
  9. Separate: dy/y = x dx ⇒ ln|y| = x²/2 + C ⇒ y = Ae^(x²/2); y(0)=2 ⇒ A=2. y = 2e^(x²/2). Check: y' = 2e^(x²/2)·x = xy ✓, y(0)=2 ✓.
  10. x ≥ x² on [0,1]. (a) ∫₀¹(x−x²)dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. (b) Washers about the x-axis: π∫₀¹(x²−x⁴)dx = π(1/3−1/5) = 2π/15.

Part 2 — field guide check

  • All twelve rows present: linear approximation; First Derivative Test; Second Derivative Test and concavity; Closed Interval Method; optimization; related rates; Riemann sums and Trapezoidal Rule; FTC (both parts); substitution; separable DEs; area between curves; volumes.
  • Each row has all four elements: when to reach for it, the rule or statement, a worked example, and a mistake to avoid. Typical good mistakes: forgetting endpoints in the Closed Interval Method; differentiating before substituting in related rates; forgetting to change limits in a definite substitution; using top−bottom in the wrong order; using π∫f instead of π∫(R²−r²) for washers.

pages.title: Answer Key - Semester 2 Final Exam
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Semester 2 Final Exam (60 pts)

Calculus Honors · Semester 2 Finals Week. Do not distribute. Score on the Semester Final Rubric (4 criteria × 15). Evidence: Part A mostly Understanding; Parts B and C mostly Reasoning; whole exam for Clarity and Honesty (honor line signed; proven versus checked kept distinct).

Part A

  1. (a) y' = 3x²−2, at x=1: y=−1, slope 1. Tangent y = x − 2. Normal slope −1: y = −x. (b) y' = 1/(3x^(2/3)). As x→0⁺ and x→0⁻, y' → +∞ (x^(2/3) is positive on both sides). The graph passes through the origin with a vertical tangent line x = 0; it is not a cusp because the slope goes to +∞ on both sides.
  2. f' = 1/x, f(1)=0, f'(1)=1: L(x) = x − 1. L(1.05) = 0.05 (true ln 1.05 ≈ 0.04879). Too high: f'' = −1/x² < 0, so ln is concave down and the tangent line lies above the curve.
  3. f' = 4x³−16x = 4x(x−2)(x+2). Critical points in [−1,3]: x=0 and x=2 (x=−2 is outside). Compare f(−1)=−4, f(0)=3, f(2)=−13, f(3)=12. Absolute max 12 at x=3; absolute min −13 at x=2.
  4. f' = (1−x)e⁻ˣ, f'' = (x−2)e⁻ˣ. Increasing on (−∞,1), decreasing on (1,∞). Concave down on (−∞,2), concave up on (2,∞). Local (and absolute) max at x=1, f(1)=1/e. Inflection point (2, 2/e²). lim f = 0 (x/eˣ → 0).
  5. (a) [x³−2x²+x] from 0 to 2 = 8−8+2 = 2. (b) u=x²: ½ sin(x²) + C. (c) u = sin x, du = cos x dx; limits 0 to 1: ∫u du = 1/2.
  6. FTC Part 1 with the Chain Rule: G'(x) = ln(x²)·2x = 4x ln x (x>0). G'(e) = 4e.
  7. dy/y = x²dx ⇒ ln|y| = x³/3 + C ⇒ y = Ae^(x³/3); y(0)=5 ⇒ y = 5e^(x³/3). Check: y' = 5e^(x³/3)·x² = x²y ✓; y(0) = 5 ✓.

Part B

  1. Let G(x) = ∫ₐˣ f. By Part 1, G' = f, and F' = f, so (F−G)' = 0 on [a,b]. A function with zero derivative on an interval is constant (a consequence of the Mean Value Theorem), so F(x) = G(x) + C. Then F(b)−F(a) = [G(b)+C] − [G(a)+C] = G(b) − G(a) = ∫ₐᵇ f − 0. Look for the zero-derivative ⇒ constant step named, and the constants cancelling.
  2. f = x³: f' = 3x² ≥ 0 on both sides of 0, so no extremum; f'' = 6x changes sign, so inflection at 0. f = x⁴: f' = 4x³ goes from − to +, so a local minimum at 0; f'' = 12x² ≥ 0 on both sides, no sign change, so no inflection. The claim is false (both have f'(0)=f''(0)=0 but behave differently). Correct statement: an inflection point needs f'' to change sign; f''(c)=0 only makes c a candidate.
  3. S = x² + 4xh with h = 32/x², so S(x) = x² + 128/x, domain x > 0. S' = 2x − 128/x² = 0 ⇒ x³ = 64 ⇒ x = 4, h = 2. S(4) = 16+32 = 48. Justification: S'' = 2 + 256/x³ > 0 for all x > 0, so S is concave up and the only critical point is the absolute minimum (also S→∞ as x→0⁺ and x→∞). Base 4 m × 4 m, height 2 m; surface area 48 m².
  4. √x ≥ x on [0,1] (they meet at 0 and 1). (a) ∫₀¹(√x−x)dx = 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6. (b) Square side √x−x: ∫₀¹(√x−x)²dx = ∫(x − 2x^(3/2) + x²)dx = 1/2 − 4/5 + 1/3 = 1/30. (c) Washers: outer radius √x, inner radius x: π∫₀¹(x − x²)dx = π(1/2−1/3) = π/6. Two radii because the region does not touch the axis along its length, so the solid has a hole (washers, not disks).

Part C

  1. (a) s = ∫v = t³−6t²+9t + C, s(0)=4 ⇒ s = t³−6t²+9t+4; a = 6t−12. (b) v = 3(t−1)(t−3): v>0 on (0,1), v<0 on (1,3), v>0 on (3,4). s(0)=4, s(1)=8, s(3)=4, s(4)=8. Displacement = s(4)−s(0) = 4 m (= ∫₀⁴v). Total distance = 4+4+4 = 12 m. They differ because the particle reverses direction at t=1 and t=3, so the backward leg cancels forward motion in displacement but not in distance. (c) s is continuous on [0,4] and differentiable on (0,4) (a polynomial). Average velocity (8−4)/4 = 1. Solve 3c²−12c+9 = 1 ⇒ 3c²−12c+8 = 0 ⇒ c = 2 ± 2√3/3 (≈ 0.845 and 3.155), both in (0,4). (d) v(2.5) = 18.75−30+9 = −2.25, a(2.5) = 3: opposite signs, so slowing down.
  2. (a) y = 80e^(kt); 50 = 80e^(10k) ⇒ k = (1/10)ln(5/8) ≈ −0.0470. (b) Half-life T: e^(kT) = 1/2 ⇒ T = ln 2 / |k| = 10 ln 2 / ln(8/5) ≈ 14.7 years. (c) y'(10) = k·y(10) = (1/10)ln(5/8)·50 = 5 ln(5/8) ≈ −2.35 g/yr. (d) Net Change: the amount decayed is y(0) − y(10) = 80 − 50 = 30 g; as an integral, ∫₀¹⁰ (−y'(t)) dt = y(0) − y(10) = 30. (e) Assumes the decay rate is always proportional to the amount present with one constant k, and that nothing is added; a real sample could differ from measurement error, or because the process is not exactly first-order. Any reasoned, honest sentence earns the credit.

Rubric (60 pts; 4 criteria × 15)

  • Understanding of the material (15): correct derivatives, extrema, integrals, volumes, DE solutions; right tool chosen.
  • Quality of reasoning (15): B1 names the zero-derivative ⇒ constant step; B2 decides by sign changes; B3 justifies the absolute minimum; hypotheses checked in C1(c).
  • Clarity and precision (15): clean vertical work, exact values before decimals, labeled answers, pages in order.
  • Intellectual honesty (15): honor line signed; proved vs estimated kept distinct; unfinished problems carry an honest note.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 24 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 24 Problem Set: Applied Optimization

Calculus Honors · Module 12. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. Let x be the length of each side perpendicular to the river; the side parallel to the river is 200 − 2x. A(x) = x(200 − 2x) = 200x − 2x², domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 100. A′(x) = 200 − 4x = 0 ⇒ x = 50. Dimensions 50 m by 100 m (the 100 m side along the river), area 5000 m². Justification: A(0) = 0 and A(100) = 0, so by the Closed Interval Method the largest of {0, 5000, 0} is 5000; or A″ = −4 < 0, so A is concave down and the critical point is a maximum. Look for: domain stated, justification beyond "A′ = 0."
  2. Folding gives a base of side 24 − 2x and height x: V(x) = x(24 − 2x)², domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 12. V′(x) = (24 − 2x)(24 − 6x) = 0 ⇒ x = 12 or x = 4. x = 12 is an endpoint where V = 0 (no box is left), so reject it. x = 4 cm gives a 16 cm × 16 cm × 4 cm box with V = 1024 cm³. Since V(0) = V(12) = 0, the maximum is 1024.
  3. Eliminate y = 40 − x or write x = 40 − y. With P(y) = (40 − y)y² = 40y² − y³ on 0 ≤ y ≤ 40: P′(y) = 80y − 3y² = y(80 − 3y) = 0 ⇒ y = 0 or y = 80/3. P(0) = P(40) = 0. So y = 80/3, x = 40/3 and the largest value is (40/3)(80/3)² = 256000/27 (≈ 9481.5). Check: P″(80/3) = 80 − 6(80/3) = −80 < 0.
  4. V = πr²h = 355 ⇒ h = 355/(πr²). S(r) = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 710/r, r > 0. S′(r) = 4πr − 710/r² = 0 ⇒ r³ = 355/(2π) ⇒ r = (355/(2π))^(1/3) ≈ 3.84 cm. Then h = 355/(πr²) = 2r (because πr³ = 355/2 gives 355/(πr²) = 2r), so h ≈ 7.67 cm. S″ = 4π + 1420/r³ > 0 for all r > 0, so this is the absolute minimum; S ≈ 277.5 cm². Real cans are taller and narrower: cost of manufacturing, shape for the hand, and stacking are not in the model.
  5. Point (x, x²); the squared distance to (0, 3) is D(x) = x² + (x² − 3)². Minimizing D minimizes the distance because the square root is increasing on nonnegative numbers. D′(x) = 2x + 2(x² − 3)(2x) = 2x(2x² − 5) = 0 ⇒ x = 0 or x = ±√(5/2). At x = 0, D = 9 (distance 3) and D″(0) = −10 < 0, a local maximum: the trap. At x = ±√(5/2) ≈ ±1.58, D = 5/2 + (5/2 − 3)² = 11/4 and D″ = 20 > 0, minima. Closest points are (±√10/2, 5/2), distance √11/2 ≈ 1.66. Look for the reason a local maximum at x = 0 is not the answer, and for both symmetric points.
  6. Revenue x(50 − 0.02x), so P(x) = 50x − 0.02x² − 10x − 200 = 40x − 0.02x² − 200. Domain: 0 ≤ x ≤ 2500 (price must be nonnegative: 50 − 0.02x ≥ 0 at x = 2500). P′(x) = 40 − 0.04x = 0 ⇒ x = 1000 units; price p(1000) = 50 − 20 = $30; maximum profit P(1000) = 40000 − 20000 − 200 = $19,800. Endpoints: P(0) = −200 and P(2500) = −25,200, so the critical point is the absolute maximum (also P″ = −0.04 < 0).
  7. A(x) = x(10 − x), 7 ≤ x ≤ 10. A′(x) = 10 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 5, which is not in the domain. On [7, 10], A′ < 0 (A′(7) = −4), so A is decreasing and the maximum is at the endpoint x = 7: width 3, A = 21 m². (A(10) = 0.) Full credit for saying that the Closed Interval Method must compare endpoints, that a critical point outside the domain does not count, and that "A′ = 0" is a way to find candidates, not a proof of the answer.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 25 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 25 Problem Set: Motion Along a Line

Calculus Honors · Module 12. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. v(t) = 6t² − 30t + 24 = 6(t − 1)(t − 4); a(t) = 12t − 30 = 6(2t − 5). At rest at t = 1 s and t = 4 s. v > 0 on [0, 1) and (4, ∞): moving right; v < 0 on (1, 4): moving left.
  2. a(t) = 0 at t = 5/2; a < 0 on [0, 5/2), a > 0 on (5/2, ∞). Speeding up when v and a have the same sign: (1, 5/2) (both negative) and (4, ∞) (both positive). Slowing down: (0, 1) (v > 0, a < 0) and (5/2, 4) (v < 0, a > 0). Positions: s(0) = 3, s(1) = 14, s(4) = −13, s(5) = −2. Displacement on [0, 5] = s(5) − s(0) = −5 ft. Total distance = |14 − 3| + |−13 − 14| + |−2 − (−13)| = 11 + 27 + 11 = 49 ft. They differ because displacement nets out the leftward motion; distance adds it.
  3. v(t) = −32t + 64 = 0 ⇒ t = 2 s; maximum height s(2) = −64 + 128 + 80 = 144 ft at t = 2 s. Ground: −16t² + 64t + 80 = 0 ⇒ t² − 4t − 5 = 0 ⇒ (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0, so t = 5 s (reject t = −1). v(5) = −160 + 64 = −96 ft/s: the negative sign means the ball is moving downward at 96 ft/s (speed 96 ft/s) at impact.
  4. v(t) = t² − 7t + 10 = (t − 2)(t − 5). A function with derivative v is s(t) = t³/3 − 7t²/2 + 10t (check: s′ = t² − 7t + 10, and s(0) = 0, so no constant is added). v > 0 on [0, 2) and (5, 6]; v < 0 on (2, 5). The particle moves left on (2, 5). Positions: s(2) = 26/3, s(5) = 25/6, s(6) = 6. Displacement on [0, 6] = s(6) − s(0) = 6 m. Total distance = |26/3 − 0| + |25/6 − 26/3| + |6 − 25/6| = 26/3 + 9/2 + 11/6 = 15 m. They differ because the 9/2 m it backs up between t = 2 and t = 5 counts against displacement but adds to distance.
  5. v(t) = 1 − 2 sin t; a(t) = −2 cos t. At rest when sin t = 1/2: t = π/6 and t = 5π/6. v > 0 on [0, π/6) and (5π/6, 2π]: moving right; v < 0 on (π/6, 5π/6): moving left. Positions: s(0) = 2, s(π/6) = π/6 + √3, s(5π/6) = 5π/6 − √3, s(2π) = 2π + 2. Displacement = 2π ≈ 6.283. Total distance = (π/6 + √3 − 2) + (2√3 − 2π/3) + (2 + 7π/6 + √3) = 4√3 + 2π/3 ≈ 9.023. Decimal check with s(0) = 2, s(π/6) = 2.2557, s(5π/6) = 0.8860, s(2π) = 8.2832: the legs are 0.2557 + 1.3697 + 7.3972 = 9.0226.
  6. v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3). |v(0)| = 9, |v(2)| = |−3| = 3, |v(3)| = 0, and v = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3. a(t) = 6t − 12 = 0 at t = 2, which is the only critical point of v. Closed Interval Method on v: v(0) = 9, v(2) = −3, v(3) = 0, so v ranges from −3 to 9 and |v| is greatest at t = 0, speed 9 m/s. The greatest speed occurs at an endpoint, not where a = 0 (at t = 2 the speed is only 3 m/s, a local extreme of the velocity but not the greatest speed).
  7. (a) False. s(t) = t³: v(t) = 3t² = 0 at t = 0, but v ≥ 0 on both sides, so the particle never changes direction. (b) False. s(t) = t² − 4t at t = 1: v = −2, a = 2 > 0, so v and a disagree in sign and the particle is slowing down. (c) False. s(t) = t² + t has a(t) = 2, not zero; for a counterexample use s(t) = t³ + t at t = 0: a(0) = 0 but v(0) = 1 ≠ 0. (A constant-velocity particle has a = 0 with v ≠ 0.) Look for a specific position function and the values of v and a at the instant, not only a general statement.

pages.title: Answer Key - Week 26 Problem Set
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Week 26 Problem Set: Related Rates

Calculus Honors · Module 12. Do not distribute to students. Graded on completion (Tier 1); use this key for spot checks.

  1. x² + y² = 100. Differentiate in t: 2x·x′ + 2y·y′ = 0, so x′ = −(y/x)y′. (a) At y = 8: x = 6. With y′ = −1.5: x′ = −(8/6)(−1.5) = 2 ft/s (the bottom moves away at 2 ft/s). (b) |x′| = |y′| requires y/x = 1, so x = y = 5√2 ≈ 7.07: the bottom moves exactly as fast as the top when the top is 5√2 ≈ 7.07 ft above the ground. (c) Substituting y = 8 first makes y a constant, so its derivative is 0 and the equation loses the very motion being studied. The relationship must hold at every moment: differentiate with respect to t first, substitute the values at the instant after.
  2. A = πr²; dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt = 2π(10)(3) = 60π m²/min ≈ 188.5 m²/min.
  3. Similar triangles: r/h = 4/8, so r = h/2. V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(h/2)²h = πh³/12. dV/dt = (πh²/4)·dh/dt. With dV/dt = 2 and h = 3: 2 = (9π/4)·dh/dt ⇒ dh/dt = 8/(9π) ≈ 0.283 m/min.
  4. Similar triangles: s/5 = (x + s)/20 ⇒ 20s = 5x + 5s ⇒ 15s = 5x ⇒ s = x/3. Then ds/dt = (1/3)dx/dt = 1 ft/s (shadow length). The tip is at x + s = 4x/3, so the tip moves at (4/3)(3) = 4 ft/s. Both rates are constant, because s is a linear function of x.
  5. A = lw; dA/dt = l′w + lw′ = (3)(5) + (12)(−2) = 15 − 24 = −9 cm²/s: the area is decreasing at 9 cm²/s. (b) D = √(l² + w²) = 13 at that moment; D² = l² + w² gives D·D′ = l·l′ + w·w′ = (12)(3) + (5)(−2) = 26, so D′ = 26/13 = 2 cm/s.
  6. V = (4/3)πr³, so dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt. Diameter 20 cm means r = 10 cm: 100 = 4π(100)·dr/dt, so dr/dt = 1/(4π) ≈ 0.0796 cm/s. Then S = 4πr² gives dS/dt = 8πr·dr/dt = 8π(10)(1/(4π)) = 20 cm²/s.
  7. After t hours, x = 60t east and y = 80t north, so D² = x² + y² and D·D′ = x·x′ + y·y′. At t = 1: x = 60, y = 80, D = 100, so D′ = ((60)(60) + (80)(80)) / 100 = 10000/100 = 100 mph. It is not 140 because the cars move along perpendicular lines: only the part of each car’s velocity pointing along the line joining them (x/D and y/D times its speed) changes the distance.

pages.title: Answer Key - Module 12 Challenge
pages.html:
ANSWER KEY (teacher only) — Module 12 Challenge (16 pts, Tier 3)

Calculus Honors · Module 12. Grade with the consistent 4-criterion Module Challenge Rubric (4 criteria × 4 points). Do not distribute.

Part A. Let one side be x; the other is P/2 − x. A(x) = x(P/2 − x), domain 0 ≤ x ≤ P/2 (continuous on a closed interval). A′(x) = P/2 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = P/4, so the other side is also P/4: a square. Method 1 (Closed Interval Method): A(0) = 0, A(P/2) = 0, A(P/4) = P²/16 > 0, so the largest value is P²/16 at x = P/4. Method 2: A″(x) = −2 < 0 everywhere (Second Derivative Test) or A′ > 0 for x < P/4 and A′ < 0 for x > P/4 (First Derivative Test), giving a maximum. The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute max exists on [0, P/2]. Look for: domain stated; both justifications; each fact named.

Part B. Base side x, height h, V = x²h = 32 ⇒ h = 32/x². Surface area S = x² + 4xh = x² + 128/x, x > 0. S′ = 2x − 128/x² = 0 ⇒ x³ = 64 ⇒ x = 4 m, h = 2 m. S″ = 2 + 256/x³ > 0 for all x > 0, so S is concave up and x = 4 is the absolute minimum (alternatively S′ < 0 for x < 4 and S′ > 0 for x > 4). Minimum S = 16 + 32 = 48 m². Interpretation: the box is half as tall as it is wide; a real box also needs seams, thickness, and a lid or handling constraints that this model ignores.

Part C. D² = x² + 9. Differentiate in t: 2D·D′ = 2x·x′ ⇒ D′ = (x/D)·x′. At x = 4: D = 5, x′ = −500, so D′ = (4/5)(−500) = −400 km/h. Since x/D = x/√(x² + 9) < 1, |D′| < |x′| = 500: part of the plane’s motion is across the line of sight, and only the component along the line of sight changes the distance. As the plane nears the point overhead (x → 0), x/D → 0 so D′ → 0: at the moment it passes overhead, D is at its minimum of 3 km. Far away (x large), x/D → 1 so D′ → −500 km/h.

Part D. Domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 5. A′(x) = 4√(25 − x²) − 4x²/√(25 − x²) = 4(25 − 2x²)/√(25 − x²) = 0 ⇒ x² = 25/2 ⇒ x = 5/√2 ≈ 3.54, and y = 5/√2 as well: the rectangle is a square with side 5√2 ≈ 7.07. Maximum area A = 4(5/√2)(5/√2) = 50. Endpoints: A(0) = 0 and A(5) = 0 (the rectangle collapses to a segment), and A > 0 in between, so the single critical point must be the absolute maximum. Assumptions to credit (any two, with an effect on the answer): the rectangle must be axis-aligned (a tilted rectangle was excluded by the setup, though by symmetry the square is still best); the circle is perfectly round with no frame or margin; area is the only thing that matters (not cost or strength); measurements are exact; lengths are continuous rather than limited to catalog sizes.

Rubric (16 pts; 4 criteria × 4)

  • Understanding of the material (4): correct objective functions, derivatives, critical values, and related-rates relationship.
  • Quality of reasoning (4): domain stated; absolute extremum justified by two methods in Part A; derivative taken before substituting in Part C; endpoints examined in Part D.

assignments.html:
Semester 2 Final Exam
Calculus Honors · Semester 2 Finals Week
📋 WHAT TO DO
Ground rules. Sit this exam in one quiet block of about two hours. Work alone. A calculator is allowed for arithmetic only; no notes, no lesson pages, no classmates, no AI tools, and no solution sites. Write the honor line at the top of page 1 and sign it:
“I completed this exam on my own, without help from people, notes, or AI tools.”

Part A — Fluency (7 problems). Choose the right tool for each problem; none is labeled for you. Show your work.

  1. A1. (a) Find the equations of the tangent line and the normal line to \(y=x^3-2x\) at \(x=1\). (b) For \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) and describe the graph at \(x=0\) using one-sided limits of the derivative.
  2. A2. Write the linearization of \(f(x)=\ln x\) at \(a=1\) and use it to estimate \(\ln 1.05\). Is your estimate too high or too low? Explain using concavity.
  3. A3. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of \(f(x)=x^4-8x^2+3\) on \([-1,3]\), showing every candidate you compare.
  4. A4. For \(f(x)=xe^{-x}\), find the intervals where \(f\) is increasing and decreasing, the intervals where it is concave up and concave down, every local extremum, and every inflection point. Then find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)\).
  5. A5. Evaluate: (a) \(\displaystyle\int_0^2(3x^2-4x+1)\,dx\); (b) \(\displaystyle\int x\cos(x^2)\,dx\); (c) \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos x\,dx\).
  6. A6. Let \(G(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^{x^2}\ln t\,dt\) for \(x>0\). Find \(G'(x)\) and evaluate \(G'(e)\). Name the theorem you used.
  7. A7. Solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^2y\) with \(y(0)=5\), and check that your solution satisfies both the equation and the initial condition.

Part B — Reasoning (4 problems). Write each as an argument: every claim earns its line, and every theorem has its hypotheses checked.

  1. B1. Assume Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem: if \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(G(x)=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\), then \(G'(x)=f(x)\). Let \(F\) be any antiderivative of \(f\) on \([a,b]\). Prove that \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)\). Name the result about derivatives that you use, and the step where you use it.
  2. B2. A classmate says: “If \(f'(c)=0\) and \(f''(c)=0\), then \(c\) is an inflection point.” Test the claim on \(f(x)=x^3\) and on \(f(x)=x^4\) at \(c=0\). Decide, for each, whether \(c=0\) is a local extremum and/or an inflection point, using the signs of \(f'\) and \(f''\) on either side. What should the classmate say instead?
  3. B3. An open-top box with a square base must hold \(32\ \text{m}^3\). Find the dimensions that use the least material. Write the surface area as a function of one variable, state its domain, and justify that your critical point gives an absolute minimum, not just a local one.
  4. B4. Let \(R\) be the region between \(y=\sqrt{x}\) and \(y=x\) for \(0\le x\le1\). Sketch \(R\). Set up and evaluate: (a) the area of \(R\); (b) the volume of the solid whose base is \(R\) and whose cross-sections perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis are squares; (c) the volume of the solid made by revolving \(R\) about the \(x\)-axis. Explain in one sentence why (c) needs two radii.

Part C — Synthesis (2 problems). These cross units. Plan before you write.

  1. C1. A particle moves on a line with velocity \(v(t)=3t^2-12t+9\) m/s, and its position at \(t=0\) is \(s(0)=4\) m. (a) Find \(s(t)\) and \(a(t)\). (b) Find the displacement and the total distance travelled on \([0,4]\); use a sign chart for \(v\) and say how the two numbers differ and why. (c) The average velocity on \([0,4]\) is \(1\) m/s. Apply the Mean Value Theorem to \(s\): state its hypotheses, and find every time \(c\) in \((0,4)\) at which \(v(c)=1\), with exact values. (d) At \(t=2.5\), is the particle speeding up or slowing down? Justify with the signs of \(v\) and \(a\).
  2. C2. A radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to the amount present: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}=ky\). It starts at 80 g and is 50 g after 10 years. (a) Solve for \(y(t)\) and find \(k\) exactly and to four decimals. (b) Find the half-life to the nearest tenth of a year. (c) Find the rate of decay at \(t=10\) in g/yr. (d) Using the Net Change Theorem (no integral to evaluate), state how many grams decayed in the first 10 years, and write the integral of \(-y'(t)\) that gives it. (e) In two sentences, say what the model assumes and one reason a real sample might differ.
✅ TO EARN FULL CREDIT
Scored on the Semester Final Rubric (60 points): understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, clarity and precision, and intellectual honesty (15 points each). Where you could not finish a problem, say honestly where and why you stopped; that earns respect, never a penalty. Keep exact values (radicals and logarithms) before decimals.

Week 24 Problem Set: Applied Optimization
Calculus Honors · Module 12: Optimization, Motion, and Related Rates
📋 WHAT TO DO
Work every problem by hand on paper, showing every step, including full arguments where a problem asks for one. Then scan or photograph your pages and upload a single PDF or image file.

Focus: setting up an optimization problem from a story, writing the objective as a function of one variable, and justifying a maximum or minimum.

  1. A farmer has 200 m of fencing and wants a rectangular pen along a straight river, so only three sides need fence (the river is the fourth side). Let \(x\) be the length of each side perpendicular to the river. Write the area as a function of \(x\), state its domain, and find the dimensions that give the largest area. Then say how you know the critical point gives an absolute maximum, not just a candidate.
  2. A square sheet of cardboard, 24 cm on a side, has a square of side \(x\) cut from each corner, and the sides are folded up to make an open box. Write the volume \(V(x)\), state the domain, find the value of \(x\) that maximizes the volume, and give the maximum volume. Your \(V\prime(x)=0\) equation has two solutions: say which one you use and why you reject the other.
  3. Two positive numbers \(x\) and \(y\) have sum 40. Find the values of \(x\) and \(y\) that make the quantity \(xy^2\) as large as possible, and give that largest value as an exact fraction.
  4. A cylindrical can must hold exactly 355 cm\(^3\) (a standard 355 mL drink). Let \(r\) be the radius in cm. Write the total surface area \(S(r)\) of the closed can as a function of \(r\) alone, and find the radius and height that minimize the metal used. Give \(r\) exactly and to two decimal places, and show that the optimal height is exactly twice the radius.
  5. Find the point on the parabola \(y=x^2\) that is closest to the point \((0,3)\). Minimize the square of the distance, and explain why that is a legitimate shortcut. There are three critical points: classify each, and say which is a trap.
  6. A company can sell \(x\) units per week at price \(p(x)=50-0.02x\) dollars per unit, and it costs \(C(x)=10x+200\) dollars to make \(x\) units. Write the weekly profit \(P(x)\), state a sensible domain, and find the production level that maximizes profit. What price does this level correspond to, and what is the maximum profit?
  7. A rectangle has perimeter 20 m, and its length \(x\) must be at least 7 m (so \(7\le x\le 10\)). Write its area \(A(x)\) and find the greatest possible area. Setting \(A\prime(x)=0\) gives \(x=5\), yet 5 is not the answer. In two or three sentences, explain why, and say what this tells you about "set the derivative equal to zero and you are done."
✅ TO EARN FULL CREDIT
Attempt every problem. For problems 1, 5, and 7, write your reasoning in words as well as symbols. Show your algebra step by step, keep your work neat and vertical, and label each final answer with its units.   1. A 10 ft ladder leans against a vertical wall. The top is sliding down the wall at 1.5 ft/s at the moment it is 8 ft above the ground.
