discussions.title: Module 9 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about how far a tangent-line estimate can be trusted. Use specific numbers as your evidence. For example, compare what the linearization of \(\sqrt{x}\) at \(a=4\) predicts for \(\sqrt{4.1}\) with what it predicts for \(\sqrt{25}\), or explain why no linearization exists for \(f(x)=|x|\) at \(x=0\).

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about the reliability of a linear approximation, not just a restatement of its formula.
  • Uses concrete numbers worked out by hand as evidence, and says which way the error goes if it can.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 10 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about the relationship between a function's critical points and its extrema. Use a specific function as your evidence, worked out by hand — for example, compare what happens at \(x=0\) for \(f(x)=x^3\), \(f(x)=|x|\), and \(f(x)=x^{1/3}\), or explain why \(f(x)=x+\frac{4}{x}\) has a local maximum below its local minimum.

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about critical points and extrema, not just a restatement of a definition.
  • Uses a concrete function as evidence, with the derivative and its sign worked out by hand.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 11 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about what the second derivative tells you that the first derivative alone does not, and choose a concrete function as your evidence. For example, compare \(f(x)=x^3\) and \(g(x)=x^4\) at \(x=0\), or explain what \(f''\) shows about \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) that \(f'\) does not. Say what the test or sign chart you used guarantees, and what it leaves open.

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about what \(f''\) adds, not just a restatement of a rule.
  • Uses a concrete function, worked out by hand, as evidence (signs of \(f'\) and \(f''\) shown).
  • Says honestly what the test or sign chart does not settle.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 13 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about when a left, right, midpoint, or trapezoid estimate of an area will come out too high or too low, and explain why. Use a specific function, interval, and number of subintervals as your evidence — for example, compute the left and right sums for \(f(x)=\dfrac1x\) on \([1,3]\) with \(n=4\), or compare the trapezoid and midpoint estimates for \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,2]\).

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about over- or underestimation, not just a restatement of a formula.
  • Uses a concrete function and sum, worked out by hand, as evidence.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 14 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about how the derivative and the integral are related, and give evidence for it. For example, you might show that the area under \(y=x^2\) from \(0\) to \(3\), found by a Riemann sum estimate from Module 13, agrees with the value the Fundamental Theorem gives, or explain what the theorem lets you skip that a Riemann sum forces you to do.

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about the connection between slope and area, not just a restatement of the theorem.
  • Uses a concrete function and interval as evidence, worked out by hand.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 15 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about what an exponential growth model can and cannot tell you. Use specific numbers as your evidence. For example, compare what \(P(t)=500e^{0.03t}\) predicts at \(t=10\) years with what it predicts at \(t=100\) years, and say which prediction you would trust and why. Or explain why the equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y^2\) behaves so differently from \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y\).

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about the reach or the limits of a model, not just a restatement of its formula.
  • Uses concrete numbers worked out by hand as evidence.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 16 - Discussion
discussions.html:
State one specific claim about how an integral is built from thin slices. Use a worked example as your evidence. For example, explain why the washer method subtracts the squares of two radii instead of squaring their difference, or why the area between curves needs to be split where the curves cross, and support your claim with a computation you did by hand.

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about how a slice is set up, not just a restatement of a formula.
  • Uses a concrete example worked out by hand as evidence, with the slice described in words or in a sketch.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."

discussions.title: Module 12 - Discussion
discussions.html:
Optimization problems promise a "best" answer, but the answer is only as trustworthy as the model behind it. State one specific claim about when you can trust the answer to an optimization problem, and support it with a concrete problem you worked this module. For example: explain why the pen along the river is maximized at the critical point and not at an endpoint, or work out a problem where the best answer is an endpoint (for instance, the rectangle with perimeter 20 whose length must be at least 7), or describe an assumption in a model (negligible thickness, perfect shape, a continuous quantity) that could change the real-world answer.

Then reply to one classmate: do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with another example or a clearer explanation. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Success criteria

  • Makes a specific, true claim about when an optimization answer can or cannot be trusted, not just a restatement of the method.
  • Uses a concrete problem with a function, a domain, and a result worked out by hand as evidence.
  • Reply engages the classmate's actual reasoning, not just "I agree."
